_meta.notes: Comprehensive index for Cuba covering Taíno civilization, Columbus 1492, Velázquez conquest (Hatuey resistance), Havana as treasure fleet hub, colonial sugar/slavery system, Ten Years' War 1868-78, José Martí, War of Independence/Spanish-American War 1898, Platt Amendment, Batista dictatorship, Castro/Guevara revolution 1959, Bay of Pigs, Missile Crisis 1962, Cold War/Soviet alliance, special period collapse, Obama thaw, and communist system under Díaz-Canel.

country_profile.government_type: Unitary one-party socialist republic (Communist Party of Cuba)

religion.note: Officially atheist state until 1992 constitution; Catholic weakened by revolution; Santería (Regla de Ocha, Yoruba-Catholic syncretism) widely practiced; orishas mapped to Catholic saints; Fidel received Pope John Paul II 1998; Abakuá (náñigo) secret society

ethnic_groups.name: White/European descent
ethnic_groups.notes: Spanish descent dominantly; also Canary Islanders, Galicians; historically dominant; many left post-revolution (Miami exile community); census categories contested

ethnic_groups.name: Mulatto/Mixed
ethnic_groups.notes: African-European mixed; significant and growing; racial identity complex; revolution claimed to eliminate racism (contested)

ethnic_groups.name: Black/African descent
ethnic_groups.notes: Yoruba, Congo, Carabalí ancestry; sugar plantation slavery legacy; Santería; Afro-Cuban music (rumba, son); systemic racism persists despite revolutionary ideology; Antonio Maceo (independence hero)

ethnic_groups.name: Chinese
ethnic_groups.notes: Cantonese immigrants (~150,000 coolies brought 1847-74); Havana's Barrio Chino; heavily assimilated; 'Chinese Cubans' distinct identity

independence.from: Spain (1898, via Spanish-American War); de facto US control ended 1902 (Platt Amendment until 1934)

country_profile.notes_unique: Largest Caribbean island; Castro's revolution 1959 (only surviving Western Hemisphere communist state); Bay of Pigs 1961 (CIA failure); Cuban Missile Crisis October 1962 (closest to nuclear war); US embargo since 1962 (longest in modern history); Guantánamo Bay (US naval base since 1903); Mariel boatlift 1980; Special Period 1991-2000 (Soviet collapse, famine); Miami exile community (1M+); classic cars; Hemingway connection; cigars/rum; baseball; universal healthcare/literacy (achievements despite poverty); Buena Vista Social Club

comparative_rankings._note: Country position relative to continent and global. 'rank' = 1 is best/largest.

current_leader.name: Miguel Díaz-Canel
current_leader.title: President & First Secretary of PCC
current_leader.notes: First non-Castro leader since revolution; engineer; handpicked by Raúl; July 11, 2021 protests (largest since 1994); economic crisis; mass emigration

former_leaders.name: Raúl Castro
former_leaders.notes: Fidel's brother; gradual economic reforms (self-employment, property, cell phones); Obama diplomatic opening 2014-16; stepped down orderly; military controls economy

former_leaders.name: Fidel Castro
former_leaders.notes: Revolutionary icon; overthrew Batista; nationalized everything; aligned with USSR; survived 600+ assassination attempts (CIA); marathon speeches; beard/olive green; Bay of Pigs victory; Missile Crisis; sent troops to Angola/Ethiopia; Special Period; longest-ruling non-royal leader; died November 2016; polarizing legacy: hero vs dictator

former_leaders.name: Fulgencio Batista
former_leaders.notes: Military strongman; US-backed; corrupt; mafia ties (Havana casinos, Lucky Luciano/Meyer Lansky); brutal repression; fled to Dominican Republic January 1, 1959

former_leaders.name: Gerardo Machado
former_leaders.notes: 'Tropical Mussolini'; dictator; extended term illegally; brutal; overthrown 1933

former_leaders.name: Tomás Estrada Palma
former_leaders.notes: First president of independent Cuba; Platt Amendment era; US military occupation followed

910.name: Indigenous Peoples of Cuba
910.description: The indigenous peoples of Cuba, including the Guanahatabey (Ciboney), Sub-Taíno, and Taíno civilizations, who developed increasingly complex societies over thousands of years before European contact.

sub_clusters.name: Guanahatabey and Ciboney Early Peoples
sub_clusters.description: The earliest inhabitants of Cuba, the Guanahatabey (also called Ciboney), were hunter-gatherers and shell-collectors who occupied the western part of the island. They lived in caves and rock shelters, leaving behind significant archaeological evidence.

sub_clusters.name: Taíno Civilization
sub_clusters.description: The Taíno, who migrated from the Orinoco region of South America, became the dominant indigenous group in Cuba. They developed complex agricultural systems (including cassava, maize, and tobacco), organized chieftain-led societies called cacicazgos, and established villages of up to several thousand people.
key_events: Taíno cacicazgo system organizes Cuba into multiple chiefdoms
Development of sophisticated agriculture and ceremonial ball courts (bateyes)

920.name: Spanish Conquest and Early Colonization
920.description: Columbus's arrival in Cuba in 1492, the Spanish conquest under Diego Velázquez, the destruction of indigenous populations, and Cuba's early role as a staging point for Spanish expeditions to the mainland Americas.

sub_clusters.name: Columbus Arrival and Spanish Exploration
sub_clusters.description: Christopher Columbus reached Cuba on October 28, 1492, during his first voyage, describing it as 'the most beautiful land human eyes have ever seen.' He initially believed it was a peninsula of mainland Asia.
key_events: Columbus reaches Cuba on October 28, 1492
Columbus describes Cuba as 'the most beautiful land human eyes have ever seen'

sub_clusters.name: Velázquez Conquest and Indigenous Resistance
sub_clusters.description: Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar launched the Spanish conquest of Cuba in 1511, establishing Baracoa as the first Spanish settlement. The Taíno cacique Hatuey, who had fled from Hispaniola, led fierce resistance before being captured and burned at the stake. The indigenous population was devastated by warfare, forced labor (encomienda), and European diseases.
key_events: Diego Velázquez begins conquest of Cuba 1511
Cacique Hatuey burned at the stake for resistance 1512
Havana founded 1519 — becomes key port for treasure fleets

sub_clusters.name: Cuba as Staging Point and Treasure Fleet Hub
sub_clusters.description: Havana became the most important port in the Spanish Americas, serving as the assembly point for treasure fleets (flotas) returning to Spain laden with gold and silver from Mexico and Peru. The city was heavily fortified against pirate attacks.

930.name: Colonial Development, Sugar, and Slavery
930.description: Cuba's evolution from a strategic military outpost to a sugar-producing powerhouse, the expansion of African slavery, and the island's growing economic importance within the Spanish Empire.

sub_clusters.name: Colonial Havana as Fortress City
sub_clusters.description: Havana grew into one of the most important and heavily fortified cities in the Americas. The massive fortifications of El Morro, La Cabaña, and La Fuerza protected the treasure fleet assembly point. The brief British capture of Havana in 1762 temporarily opened Cuba to free trade.
key_events: British capture and occupation of Havana 1762–1763
Treaty of Paris returns Havana to Spain in exchange for Florida 1763

sub_clusters.name: Sugar Boom and Slave Trade Expansion
sub_clusters.description: Following the Haitian Revolution (1791), Cuba replaced Saint-Domingue as the world's leading sugar producer. Massive importation of enslaved Africans fueled the sugar boom — over 600,000 enslaved people were brought to Cuba between 1790 and 1867, far more than to any other Spanish colony.

930.name: The Great Sugar Economy and Late Slavery
930.description: Cuba becomes the world's largest sugar producer, sustained by continued illegal slave imports long after other nations abolished the trade. The island's planter elite grows enormously wealthy while tensions build toward independence movements.

sub_clusters.name: Illegal Slave Trade and Sugar Wealth
sub_clusters.description: Despite international abolition of the slave trade, Cuba continued to import enslaved Africans illegally for decades. The last known slave ship arrived in Cuba in 1867. Sugar barons ('sacarocracia') amassed enormous fortunes, making Cuba Spain's most valuable remaining colony.

sub_clusters.name: Creole Identity and Reform Movements
sub_clusters.description: The emergence of a distinct Cuban Creole identity among island-born elites, and early movements seeking reform, annexation to the United States, or independence. Narciso López's filibuster expeditions and the Conspiracy of La Escalera reflected growing tensions.

940.name: Wars of Independence and the End of Spanish Rule
940.description: Cuba's three wars for independence from Spain: the Ten Years' War, the Little War, and the final War of Independence led by José Martí, culminating in the Spanish-American War and the contested birth of the Cuban republic.

sub_clusters.name: The Ten Years' War (1868–1878)
sub_clusters.description: Cuba's first major war of independence, begun by Carlos Manuel de Céspedes at La Demajagua on October 10, 1868, when he freed his slaves and called for Cuban independence. The devastating conflict killed an estimated 200,000 people before ending with the Pact of Zanjón.
key_events: Céspedes launches rebellion at La Demajagua — October 10, 1868 (Grito de Yara)
Pact of Zanjón ends the Ten Years' War 1878

sub_clusters.name: José Martí and the War of Independence (1895–1898)
sub_clusters.description: José Martí, Cuba's national hero, organized the Cuban Revolutionary Party in exile and launched the final independence war in 1895. Martí was killed in battle at Dos Ríos on May 19, 1895, but generals Antonio Maceo and Máximo Gómez continued the struggle. Spain's brutal reconcentration policy under General Weyler killed tens of thousands of civilians.
key_events: José Martí killed at Battle of Dos Ríos — May 19, 1895
General Weyler's reconcentration camps cause mass civilian deaths

sub_clusters.name: Spanish-American War and the Platt Amendment
sub_clusters.description: The United States intervened in the Cuban-Spanish conflict in 1898 following the sinking of the USS Maine. After a brief war, Spain ceded Cuba, but the US imposed the Platt Amendment (1901) granting itself the right to intervene in Cuban affairs and establishing the Guantánamo Bay naval base. Cuba achieved nominal independence on May 20, 1902.
key_events: USS Maine sinks in Havana Harbor — February 15, 1898
Treaty of Paris ends Spanish-American War — December 10, 1898
Platt Amendment imposed on Cuban constitution 1901
Cuban Republic inaugurated — May 20, 1902

940.name: Abolition and Emancipation in Cuba
940.description: The protracted process of abolishing slavery in Cuba, the last major slave society in the Americas alongside Brazil, through the Moret Law (1870), gradual emancipation, and final abolition in 1886.

sub_clusters.name: Gradual Abolition and the Patronato System
sub_clusters.description: The Moret Law of 1870 freed children born to enslaved mothers and those over 60, but maintained the system of 'patronato' (apprenticeship) for others. Slavery was not fully abolished until October 7, 1886, making Cuba the second-to-last country in the Western Hemisphere to abolish slavery.
key_events: Moret Law begins gradual emancipation 1870
Complete abolition of slavery in Cuba — October 7, 1886

950.name: The Cuban Republic and Its Crises
950.description: The turbulent republican period marked by US interventions, political corruption, the Machado dictatorship, the 1933 Revolution, and the rise of Fulgencio Batista as the dominant political figure.

sub_clusters.name: Early Republic and US Interventions
sub_clusters.description: The early Cuban republic was shaped by repeated US military interventions (1906–1909, 1912, 1917) under the Platt Amendment. The Gerardo Machado dictatorship (1925–1933) provoked growing opposition that erupted in the Revolution of 1933.
key_events: US military occupation under Platt Amendment 1906–1909
Machado dictatorship overthrown in Revolution of 1933

sub_clusters.name: Batista's Rise to Power
sub_clusters.description: Fulgencio Batista emerged from the 'Revolt of the Sergeants' in 1933 to become Cuba's dominant political figure. He ruled directly or through proxy presidents, oversaw a new constitution in 1940, served as elected president (1940–1944), then left office peacefully before staging a coup in 1952.

950.name: The Cuban Revolution and Cold War Confrontation
950.description: Batista's 1952 coup, the revolutionary movement led by Fidel Castro and Che Guevara, the triumph of the revolution in 1959, the confrontation with the United States (Bay of Pigs, Missile Crisis), and Cuba's alliance with the Soviet Union.

sub_clusters.name: Batista's Coup and the Revolutionary Struggle
sub_clusters.description: Batista's 1952 coup d'état ended Cuban democracy. Fidel Castro's failed assault on the Moncada Barracks (July 26, 1953), his imprisonment and exile, the Granma landing (1956), and the guerrilla campaign from the Sierra Maestra culminated in Batista's flight on January 1, 1959.
key_events: Batista's military coup — March 10, 1952
Moncada Barracks attack — July 26, 1953
Castro's 'History Will Absolve Me' speech at trial 1953
Granma landing and start of guerrilla war — December 2, 1956
Batista flees; revolutionary forces enter Havana — January 1, 1959

sub_clusters.name: Bay of Pigs and the Cuban Missile Crisis
sub_clusters.description: The rapid radicalization of the revolution, nationalization of US properties, the failed CIA-backed Bay of Pigs invasion (April 1961), and the terrifying Cuban Missile Crisis (October 1962) that brought the world to the brink of nuclear war.
key_events: Bay of Pigs invasion defeated — April 17–19, 1961
Cuban Missile Crisis — October 16–28, 1962
Castro declares Cuba a socialist state aligned with the Soviet Union

sub_clusters.name: Soviet Alliance and Revolutionary Internationalism
sub_clusters.description: Cuba's close alliance with the Soviet Union, receiving massive economic subsidies in exchange for sugar exports and strategic allegiance. Cuba pursued revolutionary internationalism, supporting liberation movements in Africa (Angola, Ethiopia), Latin America, and the Caribbean. Che Guevara's departure to pursue revolution abroad became part of revolutionary mythology.
key_events: Che Guevara departs Cuba to spread revolution 1965
Cuban military intervention in Angola 1975–1991
Mariel boatlift — 125,000 Cubans emigrate to US 1980

960.name: The Special Period and Contemporary Cuba
960.description: The catastrophic economic crisis following the collapse of the Soviet Union, limited economic reforms, the Obama-era diplomatic opening, the post-Castro transition, and Cuba's ongoing struggle with economic hardship and political control.

sub_clusters.name: The Special Period in Peacetime
sub_clusters.description: The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 devastated Cuba's economy, which had depended on Soviet subsidies worth $4–6 billion annually. GDP fell by an estimated 35%, food and fuel shortages became severe, and the government reluctantly introduced limited market reforms including legalized tourism, self-employment, and dollar stores.
key_events: Soviet Union collapses — Cuba loses $4–6 billion in annual subsidies 1991
Special Period declared — severe rationing and economic contraction
1994 balsero (rafter) crisis — thousands attempt to reach Florida

sub_clusters.name: Obama-Era Diplomatic Opening
sub_clusters.description: In December 2014, Presidents Obama and Raúl Castro announced the restoration of diplomatic relations after more than 50 years of hostility. The US reopened its embassy in Havana in 2015, and Obama became the first sitting US president to visit Cuba since 1928. The Trump administration later reversed many of these openings.
key_events: Obama and Raúl Castro announce diplomatic normalization — December 17, 2014
Obama visits Cuba — March 2016 (first US president since Coolidge in 1928)

sub_clusters.name: Post-Castro Transition and Current Challenges
sub_clusters.description: Fidel Castro transferred power to brother Raúl in 2006 (formally in 2008). Raúl introduced cautious economic reforms before handing the presidency to Miguel Díaz-Canel in 2018 — the first non-Castro leader since 1959. Fidel Castro died on November 25, 2016. Cuba faces severe economic crisis, emigration, and unprecedented protests.
key_events: Raúl Castro formally replaces Fidel as president 2008
Death of Fidel Castro — November 25, 2016
Miguel Díaz-Canel becomes president 2018
Unprecedented nationwide protests — July 11, 2021

sub_clusters.name: Economic Reforms and Mass Emigration
sub_clusters.description: Cuba faces its worst economic crisis since the Special Period, exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic, tightened US sanctions, and structural inefficiencies. Hundreds of thousands of Cubans have emigrated, the largest exodus since 1959, driven by shortages of food, medicine, and basic necessities.

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
